extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of art and architectural history; sculptors and art critics
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and observational guidance for assessing carving, composition, iconography, and moral/ allegorical representation in medieval and Renaissance Venetian sculpture and architectural ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fidelity of leafage to nature
rubrics_metrics.description: The sculptor carved the under sides of the leaves boldly to the light, literally carving every rib and vein upon them, not merely the main ribs but the irregular and sinuous veins which chequer the membranous tissue, to give the vine leaf its peculiar tessellated effect upon the eye.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether foliage is observed and rendered in detail (including undersides and minor veins) to produce a natural tessellated visual effect. Anti-pattern: leaves rendered as blunt or drapery-like curves that do not match growing leaves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finish and restraint in figure-work
rubrics_metrics.description: The face is full of quietness and majesty... the hands crossed upon the body, carefully studied, and the veins and sinews perfectly and easily expressed, yet without any attempt at extreme finish or display of technical skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer natural, studied representation of anatomy and gesture without excessive polish or ostentatious technical display. Scoring: award higher marks for expressiveness combined with modest finish; penalize over-finish that reads as virtuosity rather than truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naturalistic treatment of hair and beard
rubrics_metrics.description: The hair and beard flowing in luxuriant wreaths, disposed with the most masterly freedom, yet severity, of design, far down upon the shoulders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess hair/beard composition for a balance of flowing freedom and disciplined design — neither clumsy nor merely ornamental. Look for rhythm and purposeful arrangement rather than random curls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of narrative expression in figures
rubrics_metrics.description: The sculptor has failed in telling his story plainly, regret and wonder being so equally marked on the features of all the three brothers that it is impossible to say which is intended for Ham.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Figures should convey distinct identities/emotions to support the narrative. Anti-pattern: identical or ambiguous expressions that obscure character or role within the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Readability from intended viewing position
rubrics_metrics.description: The great series of capitals... being at a height of little more than eight feet above the eye, might be read, like the pages of a book, by those... who habitually walked beneath the shadow of this great arcade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge legibility at the real viewing distance and context — details should be composed to be 'read' by an observer at typical approach distances. Penalize details that only resolve on close inspection when meant for distant viewing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of dress and costume details for historical identification
rubrics_metrics.description: In the figures of all the three youths, the feet are protected simply by a bandage arranged in crossed folds round the ankle ... a feature of dress which will be found in nearly every piece of figure sculpture in Venice, from the year 1300 to 1380.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate costume details for historical consistency and as dating evidence; check recurrence of such features across works to corroborate period attribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fidelity versus superficial imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Renaissance sculptor... has very nearly copied the fig-tree from this angle... the leaves of the tree, though far more studiously varied in flow than those of the fig-tree from which they are partially copied, have none of its truth to nature; they are ill set on the stems, bluntly defined on the edges, and their curves are not those of growing leaves, but of wrinkled drapery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish free, inspired adaptation from mere copying: copied motifs should preserve 'truth to nature' and integrated design; penalize imitative details that look superficial or incorrect in structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate iconographic attributes
rubrics_metrics.description: A diminutive figure of Tobit follows at his feet, and he bears in his hand a scroll... the figure of Gabriel... has only in its hand the Annunciation lily. The peculiar office of the angel Raphael is, in general, according to tradition, the restraining the harmful influences of evil spirits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether figures bear traditional attributes (scrolls, lilies, fish gall, etc.) that correctly identify them in iconographic terms. Missing or incorrect attributes weaken meaning and identification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition conveying intended moral or devotional message
rubrics_metrics.description: The subjects of the main sculptures... notable for their simple expression of two feelings, the consciousness of human frailty, and the dependence upon Divine guidance and protection; the small figure of Tobit follows the steps of Raphael, just touching the hem of his garment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether scale, gesture, and placement support the intended theological/moral theme. Look for deliberate visual relationships (e.g., follower touching garment) that encode dependence or hierarchy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbols as evidence of religious feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: The principal sculptures of the capitals consist of personifications of the Virtues and Vices... there is so much that is significant in the various modes of their distinction and general representation... that the reader may profitably review the manner in which these symbols of the virtues were first invented by the Christian imagination, and the evidence they generally furnish of the state of religious feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use choices of symbol, manner of depiction, and prominence to infer the religious temperament of the patronage/period. Compare modes of distinction to assess spiritual seriousness versus formalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of mere personification where symbolism is required
rubrics_metrics.description: Personification is the bestowing of a human or living form upon an abstract idea: it is, in most cases, a mere recreation of the fancy, and is apt to disturb the belief in the reality of the thing personified. Symbolism is the setting forth of a great truth by an imperfect and inferior sign... Men who use symbolism forcibly are almost always true believers in what they symbolize.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer symbolic representation for serious devotional or theological subjects; treat personification cautiously, ensuring it does not trivialize the abstract it represents. Penalize trite, recreational personifications on solemn subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid conflating duties with virtues in allegorical programs
rubrics_metrics.description: The points of weakness being the confusion of duties with virtues, and the vain endeavor to enumerate the various offices of charity as so many separate virtues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing or evaluating allegorical cycles, maintain conceptual clarity between moral qualities (virtues) and actions/duties; avoid treating routine acts of charity as separate 'virtues' in a way that fragments the moral schema.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resist over-systematization and formulaic classification
rubrics_metrics.description: This general tendency to a morbid accuracy of classification... the love of personification... the abandonment of symbolism and the profuse employment of personification... showing itself in the Renaissance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique programs that impose artificial, schematic orders (e.g., forcing Beatitudes into cardinal-virtue schemas). Favor organic, spiritually grounded organization over pedantic cataloguing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spiritual authenticity in personification
rubrics_metrics.description: In the hands of its early and earnest masters, in whom fancy could not overthrow the foundations of faith, personification is often thoroughly noble and lovely... Dante's burning Charity... compared with Reynold's Charity, a nurse in a white dress, climbed upon by three children.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate personifications for depth and authenticity: noble, spiritually-motivated personifications (e.g., Dante) score highly; sentimental or trivialized personifications (e.g., nursing-figure clichés) are weaker.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primus gradus: Fides recta (Unerring faith)
rubrics_metrics.description: Primus gradus est Fides Recta. (Unerring faith.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as the first 'step' — foundational moral quality for the believer; consider as principal criterion in moral/ allegorical programs. Note: the list is devotional guidance arranged as thirty daily steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secundus gradus: Spes firma (Firm hope)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Second step in the MS's moral program; represents steadfast hope as a distinct virtue to be depicted or cultivated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tertius gradus: Caritas perfecta (Perfect charity)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Charity elevated to perfection; in iconography this would be represented by comprehensive acts of love rather than isolated duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quarto: Patientia vera (True patience)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patience conceived as a genuine inner endurance rather than mere passive waiting; evaluate depictions for moral depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quintus: Humilitas sancta (Holy humility)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humility presented as sanctified disposition; avoid trivializing humility into mere posture or costume.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sextus: Mansuetudo (Meekness)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meekness as gentle strength; in representation seek controlled, calm gestures rather than weakness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Septimus: Intelligentia (Understanding)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding as discerning wisdom; representations may include thoughtful poses or educational attributes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Octavus: Compunctio cordis (Contrition of heart)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sincere penitence, inward sorrow; avoid superficial gestures of penance in depiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonus: Oratio (Prayer)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prayer as a repeated spiritual exercise; in art, repetitive motif or posture may signify constancy of devotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decimus: Confessio pura (Pure confession)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open, sincere admission of faults; depict as transparent, dignified act rather than humiliating spectacle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Undecimus: Penitentia digna (Fitting penance)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Penance proportionate and sincere; art should show measured, redemptive acts rather than theatrical self‑punishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duodecimus: Abstinentia (Abstinence/fasting)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Temperance in bodily desires; symbolic fasting or restraint may be used in programs to indicate self-discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decimus tertius: Timor Dei (Fear of God)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reverent awe of the divine; represent by humility and submissive posture, not terror.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decimus quartus: Virginitas (Virginity)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray virginity with dignity and spiritual purity; avoid sensualization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quindecimus: Justicia (Justice)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justice as right ordering of relations; representations may show scales, tribunals, or fair action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexdecimus: Misericordia (Mercy)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mercy enacted toward the suffering; depict acts of compassion rather than abstract benevolence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Septdecimus: Eleemosyna / Eleraosina (Almsgiving)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Charitable giving as distinct practice; when personified, show active distribution and care for the needy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duodevicesimus: Hospitalitas (Hospitality)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Welcoming the stranger; emphasize openness and service in depiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Undevicesimus: Honor parentum (Honoring of parents)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filial duty as moral step; iconography might show respectful gestures or care for elders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vicesimus: Silencium (Silence)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contemplative silence as virtue; depict with quiet, reserved posture and minimal ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vicesimus primus: Consilium bonum (Good counsel)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wise guidance as communal virtue; scenes of instruction or counsel work well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vicesimus secundus: Judicium rectum (Right judgment)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sound discernment; represent with sober, balanced figure or judicial imagery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vicesimus tertius: Exemplum bonum (Good example)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral leadership shown by action; depict exemplary deeds rather than didactic text alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vicesimus quartus: Visitatio infirmorum (Visitation of the sick)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Charitable ministry to the ill; effective in programs emphasizing corporal works of mercy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vicesimus quintus: Frequentatio sanctorum (Companying with saints)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spiritual fellowship and emulation; depict communities of holy figures and their influence on the faithful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vicesimus sextus: Oblatio justa (Just oblations)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Right offerings as sacrificial or liturgical acts; depict with decorum and ecclesiastical accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vicesimus septimus: Decimas Deo solvere (Paying tithes to God)
rubrics_metrics.description: Decimas Deo solvere. (Paying tithes to God.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fiscal piety and institutional support represented by offerings and alms-giving imagery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vicesimus octavus: Sapientia (Wisdom)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wisdom as matured knowledge; depicted with books, teaching gestures, or contemplative poses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vicesimus nonus: Voluntas bona (Goodwill)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benevolent intention as operative virtue; reward depictions of generous motive as morally significant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trigésimus: Perseverantia (Perseverance)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enduring faithfulness to the end; in narrative cycles, show continuity of devotion over time.
